# Cedar Valley Evacuation Operations Decision

## Decision, scope, and authority
The county incident commander holds sole legal authority to issue evacuation orders after receiving fire-behavior recommendations [S01]. Supporting branches (sheriff, public health, shelter) execute specific functions but cannot independently declare readiness [S01]. Vendors, dashboards, and model recommendations are advisory only and lack closure authority [S01][S16]. Authority transfers at shift change require acknowledged incident-action-plan revisions; unacknowledged handoffs block new readiness declarations [S01]. The decision covers a 48-hour operational sequence from warning through evacuation, sheltering, accountability, verification, and readiness. Scope includes Zones A-North, A-River, B-East, B-Center, C-South, and C-Ridge [S01]. Readiness requires resolution of all hard blockers, effect incorporation, current integrated check, and incident-command acceptance [S16]. Submission or model-authored ledgers do not constitute readiness authority [S16].

## Hazard triggers and zone sequencing
Conservative fire and weather triggers govern mandatory evacuation, distinct from voluntary warnings [S02]. Zone A triggers require action within 6 hours; Zones B and C follow sequential timing based on wind-shift ensemble data [S15]. Forecast binding uses conservative ensemble values, not median forecasts, to avoid delay [S02][S15]. Expiry requires explicit cancellation by the incident commander [S01]. Zone sequencing follows: A-North, A-River (mandatory), then B-East, B-Center, C-South, C-Ridge [S01]. One zone revision is permitted under IC authority if forecast updates warrant [S01][S15].

## Population, transport, and route clearance
Zone populations are: A: 5,280; B: 8,940; C: 12,600, plus tourist estimates [S03]. Medical assistance categories (mobility, oxygen, etc.) overlap and must not be summed as distinct individuals [S03]. Survey coverage is incomplete, requiring uncertainty allowances for clearance demand [S03]. Mill Junction is a shared bottleneck; capacities of feeding roads cannot be summed [S04]. Observed exercise throughput is 1,180 veh/h [S04][S13]. Contraflow requires sheriff closure and setup time [S04]. Route-loss contingencies require alternative paths validated by current checks [S04]. Fleet reservation must match person/accommodation needs [S03].

## Shelter, medical, and accessibility continuity
Smoke-safe shelter capacity requirements define minimum filtration standards [S06]. Accessible placements must match person/accommodation needs identified in population surveys [S03][S06]. Medical handoffs require public health ownership [S01][S16]. Ridge School filter repair remains incomplete [S16]. Person-level oxygen matching is unresolved [S16]. Shelter relocation triggers activate if filtration fails or capacity exceeds limits [S06]. Power continuity for medical equipment requires backup generators with staged fuel [S09].

## Warnings, accountability, and community support
Redundant multilingual warning channels are mandatory [S08]. Door-knock timing aligns with zone sequencing to ensure receipt before mandatory order [S03][S08]. Radio interoperability is a blocking blocker; volunteer-radio identifier test remains incomplete [S16]. Receipt/understanding evidence requires community support mechanisms [S08]. Private accountability records maintain restricted medical data; public aggregation excludes sensitive health information [S12]. Self-evacuation verification occurs without publishing destinations [S12]. Retention and deletion proofs are mandatory for operational rosters [S12].

## Power, fuel, and resource contracting
Fuel and power continuity requirements address observed delays in resupply [S09]. Local staging of fuel reserves mitigates delay risks [S09]. Alternate routes and suppliers require confirmation; alternate fuel confirmation remains a blocker [S16]. Coupled asset effects (e.g., fuel shortages impacting medical generators) are not fully resolved [S16]. Resource contracting authority rests with the incident commander for emergency procurement [S01]. Cost ceilings apply to emergency contracts [S14].

## Forty-eight-hour execution and contingencies
Hour 0–2: IC issues voluntary warning; fire-behavior lead validates triggers [S01][S02]. Hour 2–6: Zone A-North mandatory order issued; sheriff executes traffic control; public health initiates medical continuity [S01]. Hour 6–12: Zone A-River evacuation begins; contraflow setup at Mill Junction [S04]. Hour 12–24: Zones B-East and B-Center evacuate; shelter intake peaks; fuel staging activates [S09]. Hour 24–36: Zones C-South and C-Ridge evacuate; accountability reconciliation begins [S12]. Hour 36–48: Verification, repair of blockers, recheck, and readiness assessment [S16]. Contingencies include route-loss activation of alternate paths [S04], shelter relocation if filtration fails [S06], and fuel diversion if primary supplier fails [S09].

## Verification, readiness, blockers, and falsifiers
Independent review classifies the package as not ready [S16]. Open blockers: North Bridge engineering inspection, complete driver roster, Ridge School filter repair, volunteer-radio identifier test, alternate fuel confirmation, and person-level oxygen matching [S16]. Component dashboards are green but bind to different plan revisions; no current integrated check exists [S16]. Readiness requires resolution of all hard blockers, effect incorporation, current recheck, and IC acceptance [S16]. Falsifiers: If any blocker remains open, the package is not ready. If a current integrated check does not cover zone order, routes, fleet, shelters, medical roster, communications, fuel, forecast, and accountability design together, readiness cannot be declared [S16].
